passages.text: How Are Stars Born? QUICK ANSWER Stars are born inside vast clouds of gas and dust called nebulae or molecular clouds. Gravity gradually pulls the gas inward, compressing it until the center becomes hot and dense enough to ignite nuclear fusion. The entire process takes millions of years and produces stars of various sizes depending on how much material accumulates. Stars are born in giant clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. The process starts slow and finishes dramatically: gravity gradually pulls material together until the center gets so hot and dense that hydrogen begins fusing into helium. That fusion ignition is the moment a star is born, and the steady glow we see from any star comes from billions of years of that same fusion continuing. Where do stars form? In vast clouds of gas and dust. According to NASA, stars form inside enormous regions called molecular clouds or stellar nurseries. These clouds can stretch hundreds of light-years across and contain enough gas and dust to make millions of stars. These jets, called Herbig-Haro objects, are a byproduct of gas swirling into newly forming stars. The jets form when the star’s magnetic field channels gas toward the spinning star’s poles, where it shoots out at supersonic speeds in opposing directions. Hubble’s longevity allows astronomers to observe Herbig-Haro objects over time. These observations show us how the jets evolve as they travel through the interstellar medium. Measuring and studying the motions and changes in shape of Herbig-Haro objects helps astronomers untangle the complicated physical processes that form them, while also providing clues about the environment in which newborn stars develop. passages.text: Stars form when enormous clouds of gas and dust in space collapse under their own gravity, creating increasingly dense and hot regions at their centers. As a collapsing region becomes a protostar, its temperature and pressure rise. If its core eventually becomes hot and dense enough, hydrogen nuclei begin to fuse into helium, releasing energy. This process, called nuclear fusion, marks the beginning of a star’s life as a true star. Star formation is a gradual process that unfolds over thousands to millions of years. It involves gravity, gas pressure, magnetic fields, turbulence, and the movement of energy through matter. Although the basic sequence is understood, many details remain active areas of astronomical research, particularly how clouds fragment, how young stars regulate their growth, and why some collapsing regions produce stars while others form brown dwarfs or planetary systems. Stars begin in enormous clouds of gas and dust Most stars originate in vast interstellar clouds called molecular clouds. These clouds consist primarily of hydrogen, with smaller amounts of helium and trace quantities of heavier elements. They also contain microscopic dust grains made from materials such as silicates, carbon compounds, and ice. Molecular clouds are among the coldest and densest regions

The core of the collapsing region becomes hotter and denser until it reaches about 10 million degrees, the temperature needed for hydrogen fusion to begin. When hydrogen starts fusing into helium, the star is officially born. The fusion releases enormous energy and creates outward pressure that balances the inward pull of gravity, preventing further collapse. The star will continue fusing hydrogen for millions to billions of years depending on its size. Do stars form alone? Almost never. Most stars form in clusters of dozens, hundreds, or thousands of stars all born from the same molecular cloud at roughly the same time. The Pleiades and the Orion Nebula are examples of relatively young star clusters. Over time, clusters gradually disperse as the stars drift apart. Our Sun probably formed in a cluster about 4.5 billion years ago, but its sibling stars have long since spread across the galaxy. passages.text: of volume than Earth’s atmosphere. Their large total mass, however, gives gravity an important role. Molecular clouds are not uniform. They contain irregular structures, filaments, clumps, and denser pockets of material. Turbulent motions, magnetic fields, stellar winds, and shock waves from nearby events can all influence their internal structure. These variations matter because stars do not generally form when an entire cloud collapses at once. Instead, individual dense regions become gravitationally unstable and begin contracting independently or as part of a larger network of collapsing material. Gravity causes dense regions to collapse The central force behind star formation is gravity. Every particle of gas attracts every other particle, and the combined gravitational attraction of a sufficiently massive region can overcome the forces resisting contraction. Gas pressure is one of the main opposing forces. Particles in a gas move randomly, and their collisions create pressure that pushes outward. Thermal energy, which determines the average kinetic energy of particles, therefore helps a gas cloud resist gravitational collapse. For a cloud to collapse, its gravity must become strong enough to overcome the pressure supporting it. The balance depends on several factors, including temperature, density, and total mass. Batches of stars that have recently formed from molecular clouds are often called stellar clusters, and molecular clouds full of stellar clusters are called stellar nurseries. Life At first, most of the protostar’s energy comes from heat released by its initial collapse. After millions of years, immense pressures and temperatures in the star’s core squeeze the nuclei of hydrogen atoms together to form helium, a process called nuclear fusion. Nuclear fusion releases energy, which heats the star and prevents it from further collapsing under the force of gravity. Astronomers call stars that are stably undergoing nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium main sequence stars. This is the longest phase of a star’s life. The star’s luminosity, size, and temperature will slowly change over millions or billions of years during this phase. Our Sun is roughly midway through its main sequence stage. A star’s gas provides its fuel, and its mass determines how rapidly it runs through its supply, with lower-mass stars burning longer, dimmer, and cooler than very massive stars. Why stars do not collapse under their own gravity Once sustained hydrogen fusion becomes established, the star enters a relatively stable phase known as the main sequence. The main sequence is the longest major stage in the life of most stars. During this period, the star produces energy through hydrogen fusion in its core. Its stability comes from a balance called hydrostatic equilibrium. This is the condition in which the inward pull of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure gradient within the star. The pressure comes primarily from the hot gas inside the star. Photons also contribute to pressure, although the relative importance of radiation pressure depends on the star’s mass. Fusion maintains the high internal temperatures that support this pressure. If the core begins to lose energy and contract, it generally becomes hotter, which can increase the rate of nuclear reactions. The additional energy helps restore the balance. This relationship is part of a broader regulatory process that allows stars to remain stable over extremely long periods. passages.text: Star formation Star formation is the process by which dense regions within molecular clouds in interstellar space—sometimes referred to as "stellar nurseries" or "star-forming regions"—collapse and form stars.[1] As a branch of astronomy, star formation includes the study of the interstellar medium (ISM) and giant molecular clouds (GMC) as precursors to the star formation process, and the study of protostars and young stellar objects as its immediate products. It is closely related to planet formation, another branch of astronomy. Star formation theory, as well as accounting for the formation of a single star, must also account for the statistics of binary stars and the initial mass function. Most stars do not form in isolation but as part of a group of stars referred to as star clusters or stellar associations.[2] Stellar nurseries [edit] Interstellar clouds [edit] Spiral galaxies like the Milky Way contain stars, stellar remnants, and a diffuse interstellar medium (ISM) of gas and dust. A molecular cloud can drift in space for millions of years without anything happening. Star formation begins when something disturbs the cloud, such as a passing star, a shock wave from a nearby supernova, or the cloud's own internal dynamics. The disturbance creates regions of slightly higher density, where gravity starts pulling more material together. Over time, these dense regions become denser and denser, eventually collapsing under their own weight to form young stars. The whole process can take a few hundred thousand to a few million years. passages.text: Astronomers estimate that the universe could contain up to one septillion stars – that’s a one followed by 24 zeros. Our Milky Way alone contains more than 100 billion, including our most well-studied star, the Sun. Stars are giant balls of hot gas – mostly hydrogen, with some helium and small amounts of other elements. Every star has its own life cycle, ranging from a few million to trillions of years, and its properties change as it ages. Birth Stars form in large clouds of gas and dust called molecular clouds. Molecular clouds range from 1,000 to 10 million times the mass of the Sun and can span as much as hundreds of light-years. Molecular clouds are cold which causes gas to clump, creating high-density pockets. Some of these clumps can collide with each other or collect more matter, strengthening their gravitational force as their mass grows. Eventually, gravity causes some of these clumps to collapse. When this happens, friction causes the material to heat up, which eventually leads to the development of a protostar – a baby star. The journey from a gas cloud to a shining star A star’s birth begins in a cold molecular cloud, where gravity gradually gathers gas and dust into denser regions. When gravity overcomes the forces supporting one of these regions, it begins to collapse. As the material contracts, its center becomes hotter and denser, eventually forming a protostar. Rotation encourages the development of a surrounding disk, while magnetic fields and jets influence how material moves and how the young object grows. Continued contraction raises the central temperature until hydrogen fusion can become sustained. Such an object may become a brown dwarf, sometimes described as an intermediate object between a giant planet and a star. Brown dwarfs are massive enough to develop some stellar-like properties, and many can fuse deuterium temporarily, but they do not sustain ordinary hydrogen fusion in their cores. This distinction shows why the final mass of a forming object matters so much. The amount of material it collects helps determine whether it becomes a planet, a brown dwarf, or a star. Astronomers cannot watch an individual star develop from the beginning to the end of its formation. Instead, they study different regions at different stages and combine observations with physical models to reconstruct the process. One important method involves observing molecular clouds using radio and millimeter-wave telescopes. Jets and outflows help regulate stellar growth Young stars often produce powerful streams of gas called jets and outflows. These structures can extend far beyond the immediate surroundings of the protostar. Jets are typically narrow, highly focused streams of material moving at high speeds along directions close to the star’s rotational axis. Outflows are broader movements of gas that can sweep through the surrounding cloud. Magnetic fields play an important role in launching and shaping these structures. Interactions between magnetic fields, rotating gas, and material in the disk can redirect some infalling matter away from the central object. Although the details of jet formation are still being studied, astronomers understand that magnetic forces are central to the process. Jets and outflows have important consequences for star formation. They carry away energy and angular momentum, helping the remaining disk material move inward. They also inject energy into the surrounding cloud, potentially disrupting nearby dense regions or compressing gas elsewhere. These effects help regulate how much mass a protostar ultimately acquires. Without such processes, models of star

The protostar becomes hotter and denser As the protostar gains mass and continues contracting, conditions inside it become increasingly extreme. Gravity compresses the central material, raising its density and temperature. The protostar’s interior becomes hot enough for processes involving increasingly energetic particles, although sustained hydrogen fusion has not yet begun. During this period, the protostar releases energy mainly through gravitational contraction and the radiation produced by accreting material. The details of its internal evolution depend strongly on its mass. Lower-mass protostars and higher-mass protostars do not follow exactly the same developmental path. passages.text: A star’s gas provides its fuel, and its mass determines how rapidly it runs through its supply, with lower-mass stars burning longer, dimmer, and cooler than very massive stars. More massive stars must burn fuel at a higher rate to generate the energy that keeps them from collapsing under their own weight. Some low-mass stars will shine for trillions of years – longer than the universe has currently existed – while some massive stars will live for only a few million years. Death At the beginning of the end of a star’s life, its core runs out of hydrogen to convert into helium. The energy produced by fusion creates pressure inside the star that balances gravity’s tendency to pull matter together, so the core starts to collapse. But squeezing the core also increases its temperature and pressure, making the star slowly puff up. However, the details of the late stages of the star’s death depend strongly on its mass. A low-mass star’s atmosphere will keep expanding until it becomes a subgiant or giant star while fusion converts helium into carbon in the core.
